audit.reasoning: Coding (fixed-dominant initial stress with trochaic secondary rhythm, rule 10/100/1010/10100/101010/1010100, non-strict because of Swedish loans) rests on the modern reference grammar Wilbur 2014, the best available description; the quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.2.1 pp. 26-27 and Figure 2.1 reproduces our rule string exactly. The record had no held file, empty 'loc' and empty 'grade'; the PDF is now on file, so the record can carry locator 'pp. 26-27, §2.2.1, Fig. 2.1' and a first-hand evidence grade. No recode needed; no instrumental stress study of Pite Saami was found.

sources.citation: Wilbur 2014, A grammar of Pite Saami, langsci-press book 17 PDF, sec. 2.2.1, full text read
sources.quote: The initial syllable (cf. §2.2.3 on syllabification) of a Pite Saami foot always receives main stress. All other foot-initial syllables receive secondary stress. If a final syllable is odd, it does not receive any stress. ... Note that vowel length does not play a role in stress.

sources.citation: Wilbur, Joshua. 2014. A grammar of Pite Saami (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 5). Berlin: Language Science Press. xiv+300 pp.
sources.quote: Foot-initial syllable of the first (leftmost) trochaic foot gets main stress; all other foot-initial syllables get secondary stress; an odd final syllable is unstressed; vowel length plays no role in stress; some recent Swedish loans have an initial unstressed syllable.
sources.locator: sec. 2.2.1 Word stress, pp. 26-27, Figure 2.1 and Table 2.2
